symptom: An x86-64 syscall wrapper emits `syscall(); return number;` -- every argument erased and the return value equal to the incoming syscall number -- even with an explicit prototype and every argument-recovery option on. 1 instance, round 7 (crackmes.one 652e6f896e7e520ff1c3db3c, kernel_call@0x78).
diagnosis: ia.sinc:4836 lowers SYSCALL as `RCX = inst_next; R11 = rflags; syscall();` -- a CALLOTHER with no inputs and no output. No inputs: the setup stores have no reader and the dead-code fixpoint collects them. No output: nothing redefines RAX, so the RAX the wrapper stores is still the one loaded from `number`, and `return number;` is correct copy propagation over an operation kuna has been told writes nothing.
decisions: The filed hypothesis ('the x86-64 syscall userop likely lacks register input/output effects') is right on both counts, and so is the captain's in-tick refutation: the fix has to be NUMBER-INDEPENDENT, because the number here is an incoming parameter. linuxsyscall's shape does not transfer -- there is no CALLIND to retarget (a bare CALLOTHER, not the `int 0x80` `intloc = swi(0x80); call [intloc]` pair), the number is not a constant to look up in the 332-entry table, and it is gated to x86-32.

The rewrite is op-level and pre-heritage, not a <callotherfixup>. cortexmpriv's fixup path can only REPLACE the CALLOTHER with a p-code snippet, and no snippet can produce an opaque value out of the ABI registers without emitting a false statement (`RAX = number + address + ...`). Inserting register inputs and an RAX output on the CALLOTHER itself keeps the operation opaque, which is what is true about it.

The read set is the one judgement in the pass, so the option carries both answers rather than picking one. `on` reads only argument registers a bounded backward walk of the CALLOTHER's own basic block proves are written first, which introduces no undefined register anywhere; `abi` reads all six, which the kernel contract permits and which a multi-block wrapper needs, at the cost of reads the function never writes. RAX is read and written under both.

Over-reading was rejected as the single default because it can ADD A PARAMETER the source has not got: R8/R9 are in the SysV input list, so on `abi` the witness's prototype grows from three parameters to six. Measured, not argued -- it is the `abi` arm of tests/stages/kuna-x64syscall.xml.

The user-op ids are resolved once per program into the ArchSeam (`simd_shuffle_userops`' precedent), because the boundary ArchContext carries no userop table. An op a compiler spec specialized with its own <callotherfixup> carries an injection id and is dropped there, so a spec-declared model always wins -- cortexmpriv's third guard, at a different seam.

No OS gate. On Windows x86-64 the instruction is also the syscall entry (RAX = number, R10 = arg1), so the RAX output is right there too and the in-block walk picks up whatever the stub sets; the pass degrades to an incomplete argument list rather than a wrong one. Naming the option's model 'the Linux ABI' in the catalog and spec is the honest framing.

Delivery is preset membership, exactly as for cortexmpriv (DIV-99): the catalog default stays `off` because the read set is a modelling judgement, and `aggressive` -- which `auto` selects under 500 KiB -- carries `on`. That is what makes the need's acceptance probe, which passes no x64syscall flag, go green.
acceptance: PASS -- scripts.repipe.verify --need x86-64-syscall-wrapper reports 1/1 pass, need closed. On the filed dataset witness `kuna decompile <crackme> 0x78 --addr ... --assert 'prototype 0x78 long kernel_call(...)'` goes from `syscall(); return number;` to `return syscall(number,address,length,address);` with no x64syscall flag passed (aggressive carries it).

sweep.method: decompile-all --json in both arms (--option x64syscall off vs on), every function body compared by address; a changed body is classified by whether either rendering mentions `syscall`.
sweep.corpus: 19 x86-64 ELF binaries / 558 function bodies -- 14 syscall-bearing images from the RE dataset plus 5 no-SYSCALL controls. 3 more were skipped (decompile-all non-zero or over the 90 s arm timeout).
sweep.result: 64 bodies change and ALL 64 are SYSCALL-bearing: COLLATERAL exactly 0. The no-SYSCALL control arm is 0-changed. Discovery IDENTICAL on all 19 (same function set, same error count). 37 of 64 get shorter and NOT ONE retains an empty `syscall()`.
sweep.worked_example: FlipVM sub_13b88: `syscall(); return 3;` -> `return syscall(3);` -- the off arm returns the syscall NUMBER, the witness's false statement with a constant in place of a parameter.
sweep.inertness: This branch at `--option x64syscall off` is byte-identical to unmodified main on all 19 binaries / 558 bodies, 0 differing -- registering the pass costs nothing when off.
sweep.honest_limit: 19 binaries rather than the ~80 first attempted: this box was saturated by concurrent agents and the first two sweep runs did not finish. The population swept is the one the feature targets, and the collateral question is structural -- the pass cannot fire on a function with no matched SYSCALL CALLOTHER.

speed.method: whole-binary `decompile-all --json --max-fn-seconds 20` on the witness image (30 functions), interleaved alternating arms, median of 7 after a warmup; plus scripts.pipeline.timeit on the witness function.
speed.single_function: scripts.pipeline.timeit --option x64syscall, median of 9: 353.13 ms -> 140.82 ms, -60.12%, within the 5% budget. Folding the `undefined16` RAX:RDX composite return that the missing output forced does remove real type/merge work, but on one 14-instruction function under load this is not a claim; the whole-binary flat reading is the honest one.
